t: Judges decide custody on one question: what's best for the child. Your job is to show — with records, not just words — that you're the stable, cooperative parent. Organization wins here. p: Class Action Lawsuits — The Legal Buffet
t: A class action is one lawsuit filed on behalf of a whole group of people who were harmed the same way — by the same defective product, data breach, illegal fee, or deceptive practice. Instead of thousands of people each suing separately, one case covers everyone. If it settles or wins, the money is split among the group.

p: Class Action Lawsuits — The Legal Buffet
t: Usually, you're already in. Most class actions include everyone who qualifies automatically — if you bought the product or used the service during the covered period, you're a class member whether you got the postcard or not. Some cases require you to opt in (sign up), and a few let you opt out if you'd rather sue on your own. The notice you received explains which kind it is — read it before toss

p: Class Action Lawsuits — The Legal Buffet
t: Nothing upfront. The lawyers bringing a class action are paid from the settlement or verdict, not out of your pocket. You never pay a fee to be part of the class or to file a claim. If anyone asks you for money to "join" or "claim" a settlement, that's a scam — see below.

p: Class Action Lawsuits — The Legal Buffet
t: Be honest with yourself here: individual payouts are often small — sometimes a few dollars, sometimes a few hundred — because the settlement is split across thousands or millions of people. Big headlines about a "$50 million settlement" don't mean $50 million per person. The claim form or notice usually estimates your share.

p: Class Action Lawsuits — The Legal Buffet
t: Most settlements require you to file a claim by a specific date to get paid — miss it and you get nothing, even though you qualified. The deadline is on the notice and the settlement website. If you moved, the notice may have gone to an old address, which is why checking the lists below matters.

p: Class Action Lawsuits — The Legal Buffet
t: Fake settlement notices are a real scam. Red flags: They ask for money. Real settlements never charge you to join or claim. The FTC never asks for payment to send a refund. They ask for bank passwords or full Social Security numbers by email or text. Real claim forms ask for basic contact info, not your life. Pressure and urgency — "act in 24 hours or lose everything."
